rows.title: NuclearLang — the language — Rules of this project
rows.summary: words, shortcuts and imports live in `dialects/`.
body: - **The parser does not change per dialect.** Dialect words arrive as data in a declaration header; framework
words, shortcuts and imports live in `dialects/`.
- **Rust decides *what* is emitted; the dialect decides *how* it is written.** The transpiler knows no target
language. What a new target needs is a generic `[options]` option, never a case of one language.
- No inferred parameters, no hoisting, no `type`.
- A changed variant of `crates/nuclear-syntax/src/ast.rs` or a public API of a crate breaks its users (the language
server, `../tools/cli/`, `../tools/code_generator/`): the workspace's `cargo test` must stay green.
- Every new diagnostic code is documented in `docs/07-reference/diagnostics.md`; every word of a dialect in its
`docs.toml` (two tests check it).
- `docs/07-reference/nuclear-base.md` holds only final rules and only Nuclear: no dialect, no target language, no
questions, no history. A dialect's equivalences are the real output (`tools/spec-check`, 0 problems).
- A new `.md` in `docs/07-reference/` or `docs/08-guides/` must be a topic of `nuclear help` (`../tools/cli/`
embeds them; a test checks it).
- `dialects/<language>/defs/` is generated: never edited by hand.
- Generated code changed: `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 cargo test` and the diff reviewed.

rows.title: NuclearLang — the language — Why
rows.summary: Why
body: - One way to write each thing, the fewest tokens, diagnostics that come with their fix.
- Type definitions so agents do not invent APIs; a dialect author adds a target without touching Rust.
- Measured: the output passes `tsc --strict`, `pyright` and `flutter analyze`; 26 files build in about 20 ms.
- Left out on purpose: reading target code, OOP as a goal, a package manager ([limits](docs/02-architecture/limits.md)).

rows.summary: Dialects reload without restarting when a `.toml` changes (VS Code watches `/dialects/`).
body: | Decorators | Completion after `@` (the dialect's: `@screen`, `@on`, `@test`...) and, inside `@screen(...)`, its arguments (`route = `) and the fields of an object argument (`loggedIn = { forward: `) from `[decorators.args]`, required ones first; hover with the list of arguments. | Generated code | The `nuclear/transpile` request: VS Code shows it with **Nuclear: Show Generated Code**. |

Dialects reload without restarting when a `.toml` changes (VS Code watches `**/dialects/**`).
Where it looks for dialects, in order: the `nuclear.dialectPaths` setting, `$NUCLEAR_DIALECT_PATH`,

rows.title: nuclear-lsp — the language server of NuclearLang — What the server does
rows.summary: What the server does
body: | Feature | Detail |
| Diagnostics | The same as `nuclear check` (codes N00xx/N01xx/N02xx) while you type. |
| Quick fixes | Each diagnostic with an exact fix (`&&` → `and`) offers a *quick fix*. |

| Semantic highlighting | Tells apart dialect kinds (`stateless`), modifiers (`get`), modules, enums, functions, fields, parameters, named arguments, Flutter widgets (`defaultLibrary`), deprecated names struck through (`deprecated`)... |

| Hover | Signature and comment of each declaration; for an external class, function, constructor or member (Flutter, Dart, bloc, dio...), its API in Nuclear notation, its documentation, the package (`flutter@3.47.7`) and the link to api.flutter.dev; for a kind, its description; for reserved words, their use. |

| Completion | Visible variables (block scope), members after `Enum.`/`Module.`, statics, named constructors and enum values of external classes (`Colors.`, `Text.rich`, `TextAlign.center`), members of a value of a known type (`dio: Dio`, `dio = Dio()`, `state` inherited from `Cubit<int>`), named arguments of the file's and external widgets (`Text('a', style = …)`, required ones first), methods of the external base to override (`initState`, `build`...), kinds and templates at the start of a line, and the public declarations of the type definitions filtered by prefix. |

rows.title: nuclear-lsp — the language server of NuclearLang — What the server does
rows.summary: What the server does
body: | Helpers of the language | The helpers every file has without a `use` (`chunk`, `uniqBy`, `Pair`...) in completion (signature and comment), hover and signature help, like a function of the project. A name the file, its project or the dialect has is never the helper. Go to definition opens the helper's file of the library, read-only (`nuclear-helper:/array.nuc`, its text by `nuclear/helperSource`), for a client that declares `experimental.nuclearHelperSource`. |

| Signature help | Parameters of the file's and the project's functions and widgets, of the helpers and of external constructors, functions and methods (`Scaffold({key?: Key, appBar?: ...})`, positional ones first); highlights the current argument. |
| Navigation | Go to definition, find references, highlight uses, rename (it does not allow switching PascalCase ↔ camelCase). |
| Structure | Outline (modules, kinds, fields, methods) and folding by indentation. |

| Projects | A file inside a folder with `nuclear.toml` or `main.nuc` (Synapsis) sees the names of the other files (completion, hover, go to definition), takes the kind of its folder (`domain/models` → `model`) and, saved, the project's diagnostics (N0301/N0302/N0303). What is in `test/` is only seen by `test/`. |

rows.title: Glossary
rows.summary: Glossary
body: | Term | Meaning | Where it is in the code |
| Nuclear, the base language | What works the same in every dialect: `docs/07-reference/nuclear-base.md` | `crates/nuclear-syntax`, `base/nuclear.toml` |
| `.nuc` | The extension of a Nuclear source file | — |
| Dialect | Data files (TOML + templates) that teach the transpiler a target language or framework | `dialects/<language>/`, `crates/nuclear-dialect/src/model.rs` |
| Language dialect | A dialect of a target language: `typescript`, `dart`, `python`, `nodejs` | `dialects/<language>/dialect.toml` |
| Framework dialect | A dialect that extends a language dialect with a framework and names its platform: `flutter`, `fastapi`, `nestjs`, `react` | `dialects/<language>/frameworks/<dialect>/` |
| Dialect chain | A dialect and the ones it extends, down to its language (`nestjs` → `nodejs` → `typescript`) | `Dialect.chain` |
| Platform contract | What a platform of the framework declares, the same for each of its dialects: `platform.toml` | `Loader.platform_paths`, `PLATFORM_FILE` |

| Header + block | The one shape of a declaration: the words before the name are kinds or modifiers, the words after it are clauses, the body is an indented block | `Decl.words`, `crates/nuclear-syntax/src/parser.rs` |

rows.title: Glossary
rows.summary: Glossary
body: | Standard library | The members of Nuclear's base types and a few objects (`Math`, `Json`, `Regex`...), translated by every language dialect | `crates/nuclear-dialect/src/library.rs`, `dialects/<language>/library.toml` |
| Diagnostic | An error or warning with a code (N00xx syntax, N01xx resolver, N02xx dialect, N03xx project), a position and, when exact, a fix | `crates/nuclear-diag/src/lib.rs` |
| Habit | A form of another language written by reflex (`await`, `const x =`, `{ }` blocks): reported as N0022 with the Nuclear form | `crates/nuclear-syntax/src/habits.rs` |
| Golden file | The expected output of an example, compared by a test and regenerated with `UPDATE_GOLDEN=1` | `examples/`, `crates/nuclear-transpile/tests/golden.rs` |
| Equivalence | A Nuclear block followed by its target block in a reference document; it must be the real output | `tools/spec-check/` |

| Brief | The short sheet for agents of the base language or a dialect; `nuclear spec --brief --dialect <d>` prints the base's plus the chain's (at most 4k tokens with `flutter`) | `docs/07-reference/brief/`, `dialects/<language>/docs/07-reference/brief/` |

| Project | Several `.nuc` files built together: a folder with `nuclear.toml`, with a `config.nuc` that names its platform and dialect, or with the dialect's marker | `crates/nuclear-transpile/src/project.rs` |

rows.title: Glossary
rows.summary: Glossary
body: | Kind | A header word a dialect defines that generates a declaration (`stateless`, `usecase`, `model`) | `[kinds.<name>]`, `Dialect.kinds` |
| Kind package | Extension kinds written on top of a dialect, enabled per project | `Loader.packages`, `kinds/<name>/kind.toml` |
| Modifier, clause | A header word before the name that is not a kind (`static`, `get`); a word after the name (`on`, `with`) | `[modifiers]`, `[clauses]` |
| Shortcut | What a dialect compresses: `use` shortcuts, auto-imports, function shortcuts, kinds | `[imports]`, `[auto_imports]`, `[functions]` |
| Auto-import | An import the transpiler writes because the generated code names something | `Dialect.auto_imports`, `emit::code_words` |
| Contract (of the dialect format) | The list of templates, the variables of each and the options a dialect can define; what `nuclear spec` prints | `crates/nuclear-dialect/src/contract.rs` |
| Contract (of a project) | What a project exposes (models, routes or calls), in Nuclear notation: `.nuclear/contract.json` | `crates/nuclear-transpile/src/contract.rs` |

| Type definitions (defs) | The public API of the target's libraries, in Nuclear notation, as packages `name@version` (like `.d.ts`) | `dialects/<language>/defs/<package>/<version>/`, `crates/nuclear-dialect/src/defs.rs` |

rows.title: Glossary
rows.summary: Glossary
body: | Project card | `.nuclear/project.json`: name, platform, dialect, language, output folder, plugins and where each kind comes from | `project::metadata`, `METADATA_FILE` |
| Project map | `.nuclear/map.md`: every declaration of a project with its kind, description and members, grouped by component | `crates/nuclear-transpile/src/map.rs` |
| Line map | For each generated file, the pairs (output line, `.nuc` line): what a debugger reads | `Output::lines`, `project::line_map` |
| Home | Where NuclearLang's files are: an install (`$NUCLEAR_HOME`) or the source tree; both have `dialects/` and `platforms/` | `nuclear_dialect::Home` |
| Module | Nuclear's unit with fields, methods, a constructor and inheritance (a class in the targets) | `Decl` in `ast.rs` |

rows.title: Vision — Constraints
rows.summary: Constraints
body: - Everything in English: code, comments, diagnostics, dialects, examples, documents.
- Errors over magic: explicit beats implicit when in doubt.
- Node.js/Express is postponed by the user.

rows.title: Vision — Goals
rows.summary: Goals
body: | Goal | Measure |
| Generated code is the expert's | it passes the target's analyzer without warnings: `flutter analyze` with `flutter_lints`, `tsc --strict`, `pyright` |
| Instant transpilation | a project of 26 files builds in about 20 ms in release; a completion of the server takes under 1 ms |
| Every error teaches | every diagnostic has a code documented in `docs/07-reference/diagnostics.md`, and a fix when it is exact |
| Every word is documented | every reserved word (`base/docs.toml`) and every word of a dialect (`docs.toml`) has editor documentation |

rows.title: Vision — Problem
rows.summary: AI coding agents and the people who work with them spend tokens and make mistakes on languages that have several ways to write each thing.
body: AI coding agents and the people who work with them spend tokens and make mistakes on languages that have several
ways to write each thing. NuclearLang is a minimal base language built for them: the fastest to write and read,
with the fewest tokens. It is not compiled to machine code: a transpiler written in Rust turns `.nuc` into the code
of another technology through **declarative dialects** (TOML + templates loaded at run time). One way only:
`.nuc` → `.ts` / `.dart` / `.py`; it never reads target code.

rows.title: Vision — The golden rule
rows.summary: (ADR-lang-0001): generated code as fast as an expert's in the target, instant transpilation (read only what is needed), minimal and readable Nuclear.
body: **Performance, speed and readability of the syntax**, for the base language and every dialect
(ADR-lang-0001): generated code as fast as an expert's in the target, instant transpilation (read only what is
needed), minimal and readable Nuclear. A rule, a kind or a shortcut that breaks one of the three is rejected.

rows.title: Vision — Users
rows.summary: Users
body: | User | Needs from the language |
| AI coding agents (Claude, Codex, OpenCode) | few tokens, one way to write each thing, clear diagnostics with fixes, a spec they can follow, type definitions so they do not invent APIs |
| Developers | the same `.nuc` in the editor as any native language: completion, hover, navigation, debugging |
| Dialect authors | add a target or a framework without touching Rust: data files, templates, a contract, tests |

rows.title: Vision — What it does not do
rows.summary: inheritance only so that it transpiles to object-oriented languages.
body: - Read or convert target code into Nuclear.
- Change the parser for a dialect: dialect words are data.
- Object orientation as a goal: Nuclear is components, modules and functions; modules have constructors and
inheritance only so that it transpiles to object-oriented languages.
- Records, a `type` keyword, visibility modifiers, inferred parameters, hoisting.
- Wrap the target's libraries: only the base types have Nuclear's own vocabulary (ADR-lang-0009); every other
library is written as it is, through its type definitions.
- A package manager of its own: a package is installed with the target's (ADR-lang-0008).
- What is not expressible yet (operator overloading, Dart 3 pattern `switch`, declaring named constructors):
[limits.md](../02-architecture/limits.md).

rows.title: Emitter options and target-specific mechanisms — Options (`[options]`)
rows.summary: `implicit_self named_args declare_ctor_fields const_collection_defaults optional_params_nullable number_separators string_quote interp_quote interp_open interp_close dollar_escape reserved_escape max_bases catch_var toplevel_statements line_width trailing_comma omit_null_default interp_bare_names…
body: `implicit_self named_args declare_ctor_fields const_collection_defaults optional_params_nullable
number_separators string_quote interp_quote interp_open interp_close dollar_escape reserved_escape max_bases
catch_var toplevel_statements line_width trailing_comma omit_null_default interp_bare_names binary_literals
int_member_parens map_patterns decimal_literals doc_in_text`
- `omit_null_default`, `interp_bare_names`: Dart without `= null` and with `$name`, to avoid lint warnings.
- `binary_literals = false`: Dart writes `0b1010` as `0xa`.
- `int_member_parens`: TS `(5).toString()`.
- `decimal_literals`: Python writes an integer literal given for a `double` (a typed value, a default, an
argument of a function of the program) as a decimal (`deposit(50)` → `deposit(50.0)`), so it prints as the others.
- `doc_in_text`: Python writes a doc comment as a docstring, so a `\` and a `"""` of the comment are escaped.
- `map_patterns = false`: Python writes `{ low, high } = m` as `low = m["low"]` and `high = m["high"]` (a value
that is not a name is read once into a variable first).
The full list with its meaning is the contract (`crates/nuclear-dialect/src/contract.rs`, printed by
`nuclear spec`).

rows.title: The emitter — Constructs
rows.summary: `{{#mods.get}}`.
body: - Generic calls `X<T>(...)` (`generics` template), spread (`spread_arg`), `x as T` (`cast`), `x!` (`non_null`).
- `method`/`method_signature` get `mods` (one flag per header word): Dart writes `Color get color` with
`{{#mods.get}}`.
- Destructuring (`destructure`/`pattern`): `[a, ...r] = xs`, `{ a, "k": b } = m`, `_`; existing names →
`pattern_assign`; a mix → N0107.
- Generators: `yields_block` → `generator` flag, `generator`/`async_generator` types, no implicit return;
`yield` / `yield_all`.
- Operators (ADR-lang-0002): `[operators]` templates get `left`/`right` (wrapped), `left_arg`/`right_arg` (bare,
for calls like Dart's `pow(a, b)`), `left_infix`/`right_infix` (parenthesized only where the operator's
precedence needs it), `int`/`double` (`num_kind`: literals, typed locals, module fields, function returns) and,
for `in`, `map` (a `Map` object) / `object` (a map literal or `<K, V>`); for `eq`/`not_eq`, `null` (a side is
`null`: Python `is None`). A bitwise operand of a comparison gets parentheses (TS binds `==` tighter);
`-(a ** b)` under unary minus. `is` gets `t` (the type's `tinfo`: TS writes
`typeof`/`Number.isInteger`/`Array.isArray`). `for_entries` gets `map` and `iter_member` (the map wrapped for a member after it: `(env ?? {}).items()`). The

rows.title: The emitter — Constructs
rows.summary: operand of a spread is wrapped the same way, in a list, a map and a call (`*([b] if c else [])`, `(x if c else y)`).
body: operand of a spread is wrapped the same way, in a list, a map and a call (`*([b] if c else [])`, `**(x if c else y)`). Constructed `Map/Set/List<...>()` locals
record their type.
- `try` as the last line returns the last line of `try` and `catch` (`try_stmt` with the tail).
- The `try` template gets `catch_used` when the `catch` block names the caught value (`contains_word` over the
emitted block): Python binds no name otherwise (`except Exception:`).

stays top-level; other statements plus an own `main` → N0113.
- `if` in lists → `list_if`. Cascades → `cascade` + `cascade_self` (Dart "", TS "$"); with
`options.cascade_statements` (TS) `x = T()..a = 1` becomes declaration + statements.

rows.title: The emitter — Imports
rows.summary: `use` shortcuts, auto-imports by free name and a kind's `imports`.
body: `use` shortcuts, auto-imports by free name and a kind's `imports`. Decided after emitting from the words of
the code (`emit::code_words`: no comments, no string text). A module is not imported if another needed
module re-exports it (`[reexports]`). A file imports an auto-import name only if its generated code writes it
(`written_words`).
Lazy imports (ADR-lang-0012: `[project] lazy_imports` and `[syntax] local_import`; `transpile_alone` for a file
alone): each block of a function body (`stmts`, a one-line `match` arm) is written between marker lines
(`lazy_block`; a lambda's body is not marked, a loop's body is flagged, a branching assignment is written as blocks).
`imports` records which names each line binds (`Lazy.lines`); `place_lazy_imports` reads the free words of each

rows.title: The language server (`crates/nuclear-lsp`) — How it works
rows.summary: It exits on stdin EOF; VS Code stops it 5 minutes after the last `.nuc` closes.
body: - **Synchronous**, only `serde_json`; the whole document is analysed again on each change (`.nuc` files are small).
It exits on stdin EOF; VS Code stops it 5 minutes after the last `.nuc` closes.
- **Dialect.** The default is `flutter`; `base`, `none`, `nuclear` or empty mean only the base language. Search
order: the `nuclear.dialectPaths` setting, `$NUCLEAR_DIALECT_PATH`, `<workspace>/dialects`, the dialects next to
the binary, the install (`nuclear_dialect::install_dir`), the source tree's `dialects/`. Dialects reload without a
restart when a watched `.toml` changes. `nuclear.dialect` only applies to files outside a project.
- **Semantic tokens:** the LSP standard plus the modifiers `kind` (dialect kinds) and `deprecated`. Named arguments
are colored as parameters (italic), not properties.
- **Types.** The type of `x` in `x.` is known only from written text or construction: an annotation, a typed
parameter, `x = Class()`, `Class.named()` / `Class.static()` (its return, `Binding.inferred`), a module field, an
inherited member of an external base (`Binding.bases` + the kinds' `inherits`). Unknown → nothing is offered.
Generics are substituted along the chain (`Cubit<int>` → `BlocBase<int>` → `state: int`). The members of a base
type are in `nuclear_dialect::library`; the emitter's receiver typing (`static_type`) is private to
`nuclear-transpile`.

- **Decorators:** completion after `@` and hover; inside `@screen(...)` its arguments and object fields (required

- **Documentation** (ADR-lang-0010): hover of kinds, decorators and words from `Dialect::doc` + the dialect's data;
keywords, `Result/Ok/Err` and base types from `base_doc`; doc comments in hover, completion (`documentation`, the
deprecated tag) and signature help (each `@param` next to its argument).

rows.title: Architecture — Design rules
rows.summary: 1. The lexer turns indentation into tokens; inside `( ) [ ] { }` it emits none (line continuation).
body: 1. The lexer turns indentation into tokens; inside `( ) [ ] { }` it emits none (line continuation).
2. The AST has no format; every node keeps its `Span` for errors and the language server.
3. The parser is generic: dialect words (`stateless`, `static`) arrive as data in a declaration header.
4. The transpiler knows no target language: TypeScript, Dart and Python are dialects like any other.
5. Data before code: dialects, shortcuts and imports are files read at run time; the same files feed the command
line tool, the language server and the MCP server.
6. Imports are decided after emitting, from the words of the generated code (`emit::code_words`).

rows.summary: .nuc text dialects/<language>/*.toml (+ defs/) │ 1 LEXER text → tokens (INDENT/DEDENT) │ loaded at run time: │ 2 PARSER tokens → AST (no format) │ inheritance, merge, validation │ 3 RESOLVER block scope, undefined names, ▼ │ implicit this, const/let, async ◄── Dialect: kinds, shortcuts,…
body: .nuc text                                   dialects/<language>/*.toml (+ defs/)
│ 1 LEXER     text → tokens (INDENT/DEDENT)        │ loaded at run time:
│ 2 PARSER    tokens → AST (no format)             │ inheritance, merge, validation
│ 3 RESOLVER  block scope, undefined names,        ▼

rows.title: How code and documents are written in this project — The compiler
rows.summary: block"); framework words, shortcuts and imports live in `dialects/`.
body: - **The parser does not change per dialect.** Dialect words arrive as data in a declaration header ("header +
block"); framework words, shortcuts and imports live in `dialects/`.
- **Rust decides *what* is emitted; the dialect decides *how* it is written.** The transpiler knows no target
language: TypeScript, Dart and Python are dialects like any other.
- **A target's need is a generic option.** What a template cannot express is added to the emitter as an
`[options]` option or a template variable any dialect can use, never as a case of one language.
- **The `.nuc` never bends for a dialect.** It keeps Nuclear's naming (camelCase, `docs/07-reference/nuclear-base.md`
§2.4) and the base syntax; a target's convention is applied to the output (`options.snake_case_names`).
- **Errors over magic:** no inferred parameters, no hoisting, no `type`; explicit beats implicit when in doubt.
- **Each stage knows only the previous one** (lexer → parser → resolver → emitter); every AST node keeps its
`Span`.
- **The generated text does not change for a tool:** the line map is recorded beside it, not by aligning lines.
- **`ast.rs` and the public API are shared.** A changed variant or signature is announced by the workspace build:
the language server, `../tools/cli/` and `../tools/code_generator/` walk the AST themselves.

history, nothing "pending". `library.md` the same for the standard library.

- A target's library name on a base type (`push`, `len`, `toUpperCase`) in a reference, a guide or an example is a

- Doubts are asked to the user and written in the reference once decided; a decision becomes an ADR.
- New syntax: decide with the user how it is written; then reference + `grammar.ebnf` + parser + emitter +
contract + tests.
- A new `.md` in these two folders must be a topic of `nuclear help` (`../tools/cli/` embeds them with
`include_str!`; its test `every_document_is_a_help_topic`). After a change, the installed `nuclear` is installed

defs/
└── dart/                          # language: the target dialect of the chain (dart, typescript...)
├── dart/3.13.5/               # Dart SDK
├── flutter/3.47.7/            # Flutter SDK
├── flutter_bloc/9.1.1/
└── json_annotation/4.12.0/
├── package.toml           # manifest
├── index.json             # what the transpiler reads on every build
└── api.json               # the full API, for the tools
The language of a dialect is the target dialect of its chain: `flutter` extends `dart`, so it uses the
packages of `defs/dart/`.
Roots are searched in this order, and the first one that has the package wins:
1. `--defs-path <dir>` (repeatable) and the `NUCLEAR_DEFS_PATH` variable (separated by `:`);
2. the `defs/` folder next to each dialects folder: `./defs` (next to `./dialects`), the one in the
NuclearLang repository and the one shipped with the Language Server;
3. the cache of packages generated for projects: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/nuclearlang/defs` or
`~/.cache/nuclearlang/defs` (`nuclear_dialect::defs_cache_dir`), shared by every project.

rows.title: Type definitions — 2. Using them from a dialect
rows.summary: [dialect] name = "flutter" extends = "dart" defs = ["flutter@3.47.7", "flutter_bloc@9.1.1", "get_it@9.3.0", "dio@5.11.1", "json_annotation@4.12.0"] `flutter_bloc@9.1.1` brings `bloc@9.2.1`.
body: ```toml
[dialect]
name = "flutter"
extends = "dart"
defs = ["flutter@3.47.7", "flutter_bloc@9.1.1", "get_it@9.3.0", "dio@5.11.1", "json_annotation@4.12.0"]
- `defs` is a list of `name@version`. A dialect adds its packages to its parent's.
- The dependencies of a package (`depends` in its `package.toml`) are loaded automatically, after it:
`flutter_bloc@9.1.1` brings `bloc@9.2.1`.
- Each package is loaded with a single version. Two versions of the same package in the chain is error
`N0214`; a package missing from the repository is error `N0213`, with the available versions.
**Automatic imports.** Every public name of a package's libraries is imported when the code uses it. If
two packages export the same name, the first one loaded keeps it:
1. the parent dialect's packages before the child's;
2. a dialect's packages in the order of `defs`, each before its dependencies;
3. inside a package, the first library of `libraries` that exports the name (the most basic one).
`implicit` libraries (always visible in the target, like `dart:core`) are never imported, and their names
cannot be imported from another package. A name of `[auto_imports]` or `[functions]` written in a dialect
file has priority over the packages. `reexports` avoids importing a library that another imported library
already includes.

rows.title: Type definitions — 4. What the transpiler does with them
rows.summary: It reads only each package's `index.json`: named like an inherited member overrides it (`override` / `override_interface`) and inherited members are used without declaring them; the definitions leaves the module open (no `N0106` nor `override`); the kind generates.
body: It reads only each package's `index.json`:
- automatic imports and `reexports` (§2);
- when a module extends or implements a class that is not in the file, it walks its `supers`: a method
named like an inherited member overrides it (`override` / `override_interface`) and inherited members are
used without declaring them;
- a name that is not in the file, the class chain or the imports is error `N0106`; a base that is not in
the definitions leaves the module open (no `N0106` nor `override`);
- a base with `kind = "interface"` goes to `implements`;
- `[kinds.<k>] inherits = ["State"]` takes from the definitions the members and overrides of the class
the kind generates.
- an override of a method marked `must_call_super` in a class of its chain (its bases, its mixins, the classes its
kind inherits) gets the call to the overridden method written for it, with the method's own arguments: after
its statements when the dialect's `[options] super_call_last` names the method (teardown: `dispose`, `close`; in
a method that returns a value, that call is the value returned), otherwise as the definitions say (`last`), or
else before its statements. A body that already calls it anywhere gets nothing (ADR-lang-0014).
`api.json` is read only when a tool asks for the full API, once per process.

- **Backend and web** (`python`, `typescript`): the dialect's `[toolchain] package_*` commands

rows.title: Type definitions
rows.summary: constructors, parameters, types, members, enums, extensions, functions and documentation.
body: **Type definitions** describe the public API of the libraries of a target language: classes,
constructors, parameters, types, members, enums, extensions, functions and documentation. They are the
equivalent of TypeScript's `.d.ts` files and `@types/*` packages: one package per library and version,
stored in a repository shared by every dialect of the same language.
They are used by:
- the **transpiler**: automatic imports, overrides (`override`), members inherited from external classes,
`implements` of external interfaces and error `N0106`;
- the **tools**: the Language Server (completion, hover, parameter signatures), `nuclear defs` and agents,
which look up an API without reading the library's source code.
The system is the same for every language. The only language-specific part is the generator that
produces the files (§6).

A field rule: `optional` (the field is `x?: T`), `list` (its type is a list, or not), `target` (its type, or its

rows.summary: A dialect is a folder `dialects/<name>/` with one or more `.toml` files, or a single file `dialects/<name>.toml`.
body: A dialect is a folder `dialects/<name>/` with one or more `.toml` files, or a single file
`dialects/<name>.toml`. All the files of a folder are merged; only one has the `[dialect]` section. The folder
can be split by topic:
nuclearlang/dialects/dart/frameworks/flutter/
├── dialect.toml            # [dialect] (with defs, §5.6), [kinds.*], [imports]
├── docs.toml               # documentation for the editor (§5.7); not part of the dialect
└── templates/
├── stateless.tpl       # template of the stateless kind
└── stateful.tpl
The transpiler looks for dialects, in order, in: the directories of `--dialect-path`, those of the
`NUCLEAR_DIALECT_PATH` variable (separated by `:`), `./dialects` and the dialects shipped with NuclearLang. In each
directory it looks at `<name>/` and `<platform>/<name>/`. `--dialect` accepts a name or a path to the folder or
file; a Synapsis project names its dialect in `config.nuc` ([projects.md](projects.md) §1).

rows.summary: Templates use a subset of Mustache: Formatting rules:
body: Templates use a subset of Mustache:
| Form | Meaning |
| `{{name}}` | Inserts a variable. `{{clause.on}}` reads a field |
| `{{#name}}...{{/name}}` | If the variable is true (non-empty text, `true`, a list with elements), writes the inside. If it is a list, writes it once per element |
| `{{^name}}...{{/name}}` | Writes the inside if the variable is false or empty |
| `{{#a or b}}...{{/a or b}}` | The first of the alternatives that is true (also in `{{a or b}}`): a section that opens for either of two variables |
| `{{.}}` | The current element of a list of texts |
| `{{@first}}` `{{@last}}` `{{@index}}` | Position inside a list: `{{^@last}}, {{/@last}}` |

| `{{name\|filter}}` | Filters: `pascal`, `camel`, `snake`, `kebab`, `lower`, `upper`, `join:", "`, `json` / `toml` (a value inside a double-quoted JSON or TOML string, escaped), `html` (inside HTML text or an attribute, as entities), `unquote` (a string argument as a bare name: `{{decor.oneToMany.inverse\|unquote}}Id` → `projectId`), `escape:"$"` (a backslash before each of those characters: `\|json\|escape:"$"` inside a string that interpolates `$`); they chain (`\|unquote\|snake`) |

material = "package:flutter/material.dart"                        # module
materialui = "import 'package:material_ui/material_ui.dart';"     # whole line, copied as it is
"fs/promises" = "node:fs/promises"

The optional `[syntax] local_import` template writes an import inside a block, for a project with `lazy_imports`

rows.summary: type definitions package (§5.6) brings the public names of its libraries and the library that provides each one, generated with the official Dart analyzer.
body: **Imports generated from type definitions.** In `dart` and `flutter` there are no hand-written lists: each
type definitions package (§5.6) brings the public names of its libraries and the library that provides each
one, generated with the official Dart analyzer. A name written in `[auto_imports]` has priority over the
packages. `tools/analyze-flutter.sh` transpiles the Flutter examples and checks them with `flutter analyze`.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 5.2 `[auto_imports]`: automatic imports
rows.summary: [auto_imports] "node:fs/promises" = ["readFile", "writeFile", "mkdir"] "package:flutter/material.dart" = ["MaterialApp", "Scaffold", "Text"] If the code uses `readFile` and the file neither declares nor imports it, the transpiler adds the import.
body: ```toml
[auto_imports]
"node:fs/promises" = ["readFile", "writeFile", "mkdir"]
"package:flutter/material.dart" = ["MaterialApp", "Scaffold", "Text"]
If the code uses `readFile` and the file neither declares nor imports it, the transpiler adds the import. The
names of the same module are grouped in a single line (`import { readFile, writeFile } from ...`) when the
target defines `import_names`; otherwise the whole module is imported (Dart). A symbol can come from only one
module.
`[reexports]` says which modules fully include others. A module is not imported if another module the file
already imports includes it:
```toml
[reexports]
"package:flutter/material.dart" = ["package:flutter/widgets.dart"]
With `Scaffold` (material) and `Text` (widgets) only `material.dart` is imported; with `Text` alone,
`widgets.dart`.
A project may declare a name a library also exports (`Task` next to fpdart's `Task`): the import of that library
gets a `hide` clause with the project's names when the dialect's `import_default` writes `clauses.hide`. The names
come from the type definitions, and from `[exports]` for a library without them:
```toml
[exports]
"package:fpdart/fpdart.dart" = ["Task", "Option", "State", "Unit"]

body: ```toml
[functions]
print = "console.log"                         # renames the function
now = { template = "new Date()" }             # replaces the whole call
sleep = { template = "await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, {{arg0}}))" }
The template receives `args` (the positional arguments), `arg0`, `arg1`... and `call_args` (every argument, a named
one as the dialect's `named_arg` writes it: Python's `print(line, flush=True)`), and `shown` (the positional arguments
as Nuclear prints them, through `[syntax] show_double`, `show_nullable` and `show_bool` when the dialect has them:
TypeScript's `print` is `console.log({{shown}})`).
#### 5.3.1 `[call_site]`: where a call was written
```toml
[call_site.Log]
arg = "at"
text = "{{component}} › {{kind}} › {{module}}.{{method}} · {{path}}.nuc:{{line}}"
Each `Log.<method>(...)` call also receives the named argument `arg`, a constant text with `text` rendered
where the call is. Variables: `path` (the file in the project, without extension; empty outside a project),
`line` (its line in the `.nuc`), `component` (the folder under `[architecture] scope`), `kind`, `module` (the
declaration) and `method` (the function or method; a lambda takes its method's). It is not added if the call
already writes it or if `Log` is a name of the file. It is a literal: it costs nothing at run time.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 5.6 Type definitions (`defs`)
rows.summary: Like TypeScript's `.d.ts` files and `@types/*` packages: the public API of the target's libraries, one package per library and version, in a repository shared by every dialect of the same language (`defs/<language>/<package>/<version>/`).
body: Like TypeScript's `.d.ts` files and `@types/*` packages: the public API of the target's libraries, one package
per library and version, in a repository shared by every dialect of the same language
(`defs/<language>/<package>/<version>/`). The format, the priority order and the tools are in
[definitions.md](definitions.md).
```toml
[dialect]
name = "flutter"
extends = "dart"
defs = ["flutter@3.47.7", "flutter_bloc@9.1.1", "get_it@9.3.0", "dio@5.11.1", "json_annotation@4.12.0"]
A dialect adds its packages to its parent's and the dependencies of each package are loaded automatically.
With them the transpiler:
- imports each public name of their libraries by itself (§5.2);
- marks as an override (`override` / `override_interface`) a method named like a member of an external class
the module extends or implements, and lets inherited members be used without declaring them;
- gives error `N0106` for a name that is not in the file nor in the class chain;
- sends a base with `kind = "interface"` to `implements` (in Dart, an `interface class` like `Comparable`).
`[options] implicit_base` names the class every class extends in the target (Dart: `Object`), so `toString()`
is also marked as an override.

rows.summary: 5.8 `[library.<base>]`: the standard library
body: | Key | Use |

| bases | `string`, `list`, `map`, `set`, `int`, `double`, `number` (what `int` and `double` share), `boolean`, `bytes`, `datetime`, `duration`, `regex`, `match`, `error`, `any` (`toString`); objects `Math`, `Json`, `String`, `DateTime`, `Duration`, `Regex`, `Set`, `Bytes`, `Error` (`new` is the constructor) |

| variables | `recv` (the value before the dot), `args`, `arg0`..., `has_args`, `n`, `named.<name>` (a named argument; a literal `true`/`false` is a flag), `call_args` (every argument as the target writes a call), `argN_is.<base>` (the static type of an argument: `split` takes a string or a Regex), `elem` (the element type), `type_args`, and for the first expression lambda among the arguments `fn.param`, `fn.params`, `fn.p0`, `fn.p1`, `fn.body`, `fn.cond` (the body where a condition goes: a conditional expression keeps its parentheses) |

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 5.8 `[library.<base>]`: the standard library
rows.summary: `[syntax] renamed_params` (optional, usually `{ template, helper }`): a parameter renamed because it would hide a function of the target (`list` → `list_`) keeps its own name outside.
body: `[syntax] renamed_params` (optional, usually `{ template, helper }`): a parameter renamed because it would hide a
function of the target (`list` → `list_`) keeps its own name outside. Its template gets `renamed` (a list of `{ name,
local }`) and is written into `public_names` of the `function` and `method` templates that place that variable (Python:
`@_public_names(list_="list")` above the `def`).
| extensions | A member Nuclear does not define (`[library.string] tr` in the mobile platform) is the dialect's own: rendered the same way, its result type unknown |
The emitter rewrites a member when the receiver's type is known (`nuclear-base.md`'s types, a literal, a library
result, a declared or alias signature, `inject<T>()`, a `Result`'s `value`/`error`, the parameters of a callback
from the receiver's element type). A target's name on a base type is N0114 (`library::WRONG`); a method of a value
without a type whose templates differ between bases is N0115; a property of a value without a type is the value's
own and is written as it is. The platform contract does not list library members: every language dialect renders
the whole vocabulary (`nuclear spec` prints it).

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 6. Validation
rows.summary: `nuclear dialect check <name>` validates a dialect and every dialect it extends.
body: `nuclear dialect check <name>` validates a dialect and every dialect it extends. The transpiler applies the
same rules every time it loads a dialect:
| Rule | Code |
| Valid TOML, known sections and keys, values of the right type, well-formed templates | N0206 |
| A shortcut is defined only once across the dialect's files | N0204 |
| A child dialect does not redefine a parent's shortcut, unless it lists it in `[dialect] replaces` | N0204 |
| Kinds, modifiers and clauses share a namespace | N0204 |
| `[functions]` and `[auto_imports]` share a namespace | N0204 |
| A symbol of `[auto_imports]` comes from a single module | N0204 |
| No shortcut is named like a reserved word of the base language | N0212 |
| Two shortcuts that differ only in case or in one character (names of 6+ letters) | N0205 (warning) |
| A template uses a variable that does not exist | N0210 (warning) |
| A target dialect defines every required template | N0203 |
| The dialect exists and inheritance has no cycles | N0207 |
Example: `nestjs` inherits from `nodejs`, which imports `Transform` from `node:stream`. In Nest, `Transform` is
the decorator of `class-transformer`; so `nestjs` declares `replaces = ["auto_imports.Transform"]`.

the dialect it extends, source "package" without a version), and a Synapsis project names it in `config.nuc`

rows.summary: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries (ADR-synapsis-0004): the native kinds of a platform live in its contract (§1), and platform, with TOML and templates only.
body: Kinds are Nuclear's libraries (ADR-synapsis-0004): the **native** kinds of a platform live in its contract (§1), and
**extension** kinds come in packages, written by a project or by the community on top of the dialects of one

├── kind.toml                 [package] name, version, platform, description
├── docs.toml                 editor documentation of its words (§5.7)
├── fastapi/kind.toml         how the fastapi dialect writes its kinds: [plugin] (runtime packages, defs, names)

name = "jobs"
version = "0.1.0"
platform = "backend"
description = "Scheduled jobs of the app."

body: A new dialect (a language like `crystal` or a framework like `amber`) is created by a **coding agent**
(Claude, Codex, OpenCode...) following this section. Whoever asks for it describes the *what for* and reviews

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 8.1 Purpose and philosophy
rows.summary: every target.
body: - Nuclear is a cross-cutting transpiler: the parser, the AST, the analysis and the emitter are the same for
every target. A dialect **only teaches how** each construct is written in its target.
- Golden rule (above): the generated code is an expert's in the target, transpiling is immediate and what is
written in Nuclear is the minimum.
- Rust decides *what* is emitted; the dialect decides *how* it is written.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 8.2 What a dialect can do
rows.summary: Only what sections 1–6 describe, with files in `dialects/<name>/`: A target dialect defines every required template (`nuclear spec` lists them).
body: Only what sections 1–6 describe, with files in `dialects/<name>/`:
| File | Content |

| `dialect.toml` | `[dialect]` (`name`, `extends`, `replaces`, `defs`), `[syntax]`, `[types]`, `[operators]`, `[options]`, `[imports]`, `[auto_imports]`, `[functions]`, `[call_site]`, `[kinds.*]`, `[modifiers]`, `[clauses]`, `[decorators]`, `[names]`, `[project]`, `[architecture]` |
| `templates/*.tpl` | long templates, with the Mustache subset of §4 |
| `keywords.toml` | reserved words of the target (escaped automatically) |
| `spec.md` | the rules the dialect adds to the base, its translation table and the equivalences of the base examples |
A target dialect defines every required template (`nuclear spec` lists them). A framework dialect extends a
target (or another framework) and adds kinds, decorators and shortcuts.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 8.3 Process
rows.summary: 1. Read the contract: `nuclear spec` (base language, this document and the list of templates, variables and options).
body: 1. **Read the contract:** `nuclear spec` (base language, this document and the list of templates, variables
and options). For a framework, `nuclear spec --dialect <parent>`.
2. **Take a reference:** a target dialect starts from the structure of `nuclearlang/dialects/typescript/` or
`nuclearlang/dialects/dart/`; a framework one, from `nuclearlang/dialects/typescript/frameworks/nestjs/` or `nuclearlang/dialects/dart/frameworks/flutter/`.
3. **Write `spec.md` first**, with each rule and its example: a ` ```nuclear ` block followed by the block of
the target that must come out. Each rule has at least one example.
4. **Write `dialect.toml` and the templates** until `nuclear dialect check <path> --json` has no errors, and
`docs.toml` with the editor documentation of each word (§5.7).
5. **Compile each example** with `nuclear build <file.nuc> --dialect <path>` and compare with `spec.md`. If
it differs, fix the template, not the example (unless the example is badly written in the target).
6. **Validate in the target:** the output compiles and passes the target's analyzer or linter without
warnings.
7. **Deliver** the list of base constructs covered, the ones that could not be expressed and why.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 8.4 Restrictions
rows.summary: 1. Touch the transpiler (`crates/`, the parser, the AST, the emitter) nor Nuclear's grammar.
body: 1. **Touch the transpiler** (`crates/`, the parser, the AST, the emitter) nor Nuclear's grammar. If a
construct cannot be written with templates and options, it stops and reports it; it does not fake it.
2. **Change Nuclear's syntax**: no new words outside kinds, modifiers, clauses and decorators, nor another
meaning for a base construct.
3. **Edit the shipped dialects** (`typescript`, `dart`, `nodejs`, `nestjs`, `flutter`). They are extended.
4. **Redefine a parent's shortcut** without `[dialect] replaces` (N0204), nor name a shortcut like a reserved
word of the base (N0212).
5. **Offer a second way of writing the same thing.** A kind, decorator or shortcut exists only if it removes
repeated code of the target.
6. **Generate code an expert in the target would not write**: no reflection, no unused layers or indirections,
no warnings from the target's analyzer.
7. **Leave a rule without an example**, nor an example whose output is not the transpiler's real one.
8. **Write in `spec.md` anything that is not a final rule**: no questions, assumptions, pending items nor
history. Doubts are asked to whoever requested the dialect.
9. **Leave Synapsis's rules** in a Synapsis dialect: components, layers, architecture kinds and

rows.summary: `[architecture]` rules are those of flutter.md §1, §3, §4 and §6, applied to its technology.
body: `[architecture]` rules are those of [flutter.md](../../dialects/dart/docs/07-reference/flutter.md) §1, §3, §4 and §6, applied to its technology.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 8.5 Done
rows.summary: 8.5 Done
body: - `nuclear dialect check <path> --json` without errors.
- Each example of `spec.md` gives exactly its output.
- The output passes the target's compiler and analyzer without warnings.
- `nuclear spec --dialect <name>` prints the base followed by the specs of the chain.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — 9. Tools
rows.summary: The transpiler loads dialects at run time and exposes a single diagnostics function (`nuclear_transpile::check`), the same one `nuclear check --dialect <name> --json` and the Language Server use.
body: The transpiler loads dialects at run time and exposes a single diagnostics function
(`nuclear_transpile::check`), the same one `nuclear check --dialect <name> --json` and the Language Server use.
So the editor marks, while the developer or the agent writes, the errors of the base language and those of the
active dialect: unknown kinds with a suggestion (`N0201`), kinds without their required methods (`N0209`),
invalid `use` clauses (`N0211`) and missing templates (`N0203`).
Editors have a base extension for every dialect (Language Server, highlighting, theme, metrics, line map) and
one extension per framework to run and debug with its tools (Synapsis for Flutter). The base knows no
language: a file's dialect comes from its project (`nuclear.toml` or the dialect's `[project] marker`) and the
links to the API reference from `[docs]`:
```toml
[docs]
"dart:" = "https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/dart-{{library}}/{{name}}{{#class}}-class{{/class}}.html"
`dart:convert` + `jsonDecode` → `https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/dart-convert/jsonDecode.html`. A new dialect
works in the editor without changing the base extension.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects — Golden rule
rows.summary: Every dialect (target, framework or project) follows NuclearLang's golden rule (nuclear-base.md §1): performance, speed and readability of the syntax.
body: Every dialect (target, framework or project) follows NuclearLang's golden rule
([nuclear-base.md §1](nuclear-base.md)): **performance, speed and readability of the syntax**.
- **Performance:** the generated code is what an expert in the target would write so it runs as fast as
possible (`const` constructors, no layers nor indirections that add nothing at run time, no reflection).
The architecture a kind generates exists in the output only if the application uses it.
- **Speed:** transpiling is immediate (the transpiler reads only the index of each definitions package) and
the generated code compiles without extra steps the developer has to remember.
- **Readability:** what is written in Nuclear is the minimum. A kind or shortcut exists to remove repeated
code, never to add a second way of writing the same thing.

rows.title: NuclearLang dialects
rows.summary: A dialect is a set of TOML files that teaches the transpiler a target language or a framework.
body: A **dialect** is a set of TOML files that teaches the transpiler a target language or a framework. The base
transpiler (lexer, parser, resolver and emitter) knows no target language: everything it writes comes from
the templates and tables of the active dialect. Dialects are read at run time, so they can be created or
changed without recompiling the transpiler.
Every dialect uses the same format, described in this document. The full tables of templates, variables and
options are generated by the transpiler: `nuclear spec`.

rows.title: Transpiler architecture — 1. Stages
rows.summary: .nuc text dialects/<name>/*.toml │ 1. LEXER text → tokens │ │ 2. PARSER tokens → AST │ loaded at run time │ 3. RESOLVER block scopes, undefined │ (inheritance, collisions, validation) │ names, implicit this, ▼ │ const/let, async, returns ◄── Dialect: kinds, shortcuts, auto-imports │ 4. EMITTER AST…
body: .nuc text                                    dialects/<name>/*.toml
│  1. LEXER      text   → tokens                 │
│  2. PARSER     tokens → AST                    │  loaded at run time
│  3. RESOLVER   block scopes, undefined         │  (inheritance, collisions, validation)
│                names, implicit this,           ▼
│                const/let, async, returns ◄── Dialect: kinds, shortcuts, auto-imports
│  4. EMITTER    AST → dialect templates   ◄── [syntax] [types] [operators]
.ts / .dart / ... text
Each stage knows only the previous one. Diagnostics accumulate in all of them and come out as text or JSON.

rows.title: Transpiler architecture — 2. Design rules
rows.summary: 1. The lexer produces indentation as tokens.
body: 1. **The lexer produces indentation as tokens.** `INDENT`/`DEDENT` let the parser work as if there were braces.
Inside `( ) [ ] { }` they are not emitted (line continuation).
2. **The AST has no format.** No `;`, no spaces, no braces. Each node keeps its `Span` (position in the file)
for errors and for the LSP.
3. **The parser is generic.** It knows nothing about Flutter or NestJS. A dialect's words (`stateless`,
`extension`, `static`...) arrive as data in the declaration's header and the dialect validates them.
4. **The transpiler knows no target language.** TypeScript and Dart are dialects like any other: files with
templates. The Rust code decides *what* to emit (a constant, a `this`, an `await`); the dialect decides *how*
it is written.
5. **Data before code.** Dialects, shortcuts and automatic imports live in TOML files read at run time. The same
files feed the CLI, the LSP and the future MCP server.

rows.title: Transpiler architecture — 3. Dialects
rows.summary: A dialect is a folder `dialects/<name>/` with TOML files (full format in nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/dialects.md).
body: A dialect is a folder `dialects/<name>/` with TOML files (full format in [nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/dialects.md](../07-reference/dialects.md)).
Dialects inherit:
typescript ──► nodejs ──► nestjs
dart ───────► flutter
- **Target** (`typescript`, `dart`): templates for each construct of the base language, types, operators,
options and reserved words.
- **Framework** (`nodejs`, `nestjs`, `flutter`): kinds (`stateless`, `controller`), `use` shortcuts, automatic
imports and function shortcuts.
- **Project**: any developer extends a framework with their own shortcuts and kinds.
The loader merges the files, applies inheritance and validates: shortcut collisions, similar names, unknown
template variables and missing templates. `nuclear spec` publishes the whole contract (which templates exist and
which variables each one receives) so an agent can write a new dialect.

rows.title: Creating a dialect with an agent — 5. What the agent cannot do
rows.summary: The full restrictions are in nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/dialects.md §8.4. The ones that matter most when reviewing: out of a template, the agent tells you; that change is made by the NuclearLang team.
body: The full restrictions are in [nuclearlang/docs/07-reference/dialects.md §8.4](../07-reference/dialects.md). The ones that matter most when
reviewing:
- **It does not touch the transpiler nor Nuclear's syntax.** If the target needs something that does not come
out of a template, the agent tells you; that change is made by the NuclearLang team.
- **It does not edit the shipped dialects** (`typescript`, `dart`, `nodejs`, `nestjs`, `flutter`): it extends
them.
- **It does not invent a second way of writing the same thing**: each kind removes repeated code.
- **It leaves no rule without an example** nor examples that are not the real output.
- **It writes everything in English**: the TOML comments, the templates, the examples and `spec.md`.
- **It does not generate code an expert in the target would not write** (reflection, unused layers, compiler
warnings).
If you see any of this in what it delivered, ask it to fix it quoting the restriction.

rows.summary: dart run bin/defs.dart --project <dir> --out <package folder> --name <n> --version <v> [--description <text>] [--depends <n@v>]... [--implicit <library>]... [--exclude <folder>]... `package:flutter/...` and the pub packages).
body: ```sh
dart run bin/defs.dart --project <dir> --out <package folder> --name <n> --version <v>
[--description <text>] [--depends <n@v>]... [--implicit <library>]... [--exclude <folder>]...
<library>...
- `--project`: the folder whose `package_config` resolves the libraries (`.` for Dart's, `flutter_project` for
`package:flutter/...` and the pub packages).
- `--exclude`: packages already generated (the dependencies): their declarations are not repeated and their
libraries count for `reexports`.
- `--implicit`: libraries that are always visible (`dart:core`).
`defs.dart` also writes `must_call_super` for a method annotated `@mustCallSuper` (in `api.json`'s member and in
`index.json`'s class): `last` when its documentation says an override ends with the call to it (`dispose`,
`deactivate`), `first` otherwise. The emitter writes that call in an override that lacks it, last for the methods
the dialect's `[options] super_call_last` names (teardown: `dispose`, `close`...), which wins over this position
(ADR-lang-0014).
`flutter_project/` is an empty project that only resolves the packages; it is also where
the mobile platform's `analyze-flutter.sh` writes the generated code (`lib/generated/`).

rows.title: tools/defs — Other languages
rows.summary: The same format for every language; only the generator changes: Both write `params` (the unnamed constructor) and `results` (methods that return a `Result`) in `index.json`.
body: The same format for every language; only the generator changes:
| Language | Generator | Regenerate |
| Python | `tools/defs/python/gen.py` (`inspect` over the installed modules of `tools/python/.venv`) | `tools/defs/python/generate.sh` |
| TypeScript | `tools/defs/typescript/gen.js` (the TypeScript compiler over the `.d.ts` in `tools/node/node_modules`; `--lib es2022` for the standard library) | `tools/defs/typescript/generate.sh` |
Both write `params` (the unnamed constructor) and `results` (methods that return a `Result`) in `index.json`.
`gen.js` also writes `defaults`: a package's default export (`export default`, `export =`), one more symbol called as
the package declares it or, when that is no name to write, like the module. With no module named, `gen.py
--distribution <package>` describes the modules that package installs and `gen.js --package <package>` the package's
own module.
Neither writes `must_call_super`: Python and TypeScript have no annotation that asks an override to call the method
it overrides.
